title: Do I have a bad ignition coil? Measurements inside
author: Stefan Bogdanescu

content:
When diagnosing an engine misfire on a platform like the LS1, it is tempting to treat every cylinder as an isolated component and assume that measuring resistance across pins will reveal a "bad" coil immediately. While this approach seems logical from a debugging perspective—much like checking hardware voltages in embedded systems before diving into firmware—it often misses the fundamental architecture of how these ignition coils actually operate. The data you gathered provides a clear picture, but interpreting it requires understanding the internal topology rather than just looking for statistical outliers.

The core issue lies in the assumption that measuring resistance across all pin combinations is sufficient to determine coil health. In modern sequential firing systems like the LS1, the ignition coils are not simple point-to-point transformers; they are part of a complex switching network driven by the Powertrain Control Module (PCM). Each coil has two windings: a primary winding that connects to the PCM's driver transistor and a secondary winding that generates the high voltage for the spark plug.

Looking at your Fluke 87 V measurements, we can see a pattern that reveals why raw resistance tables can be misleading without context. The values you measured between pins A-C and B-D (and their counterparts) represent the series combination of the primary and secondary windings when connected in specific configurations. For instance, a reading around 31–34 kΩ typically represents one winding path, while the higher readings near 82–95 kΩ likely represent the combined impedance of multiple paths or different terminal pairs. The fact that your "New Coil #1" shows significantly lower resistance (around 26 kΩ and 73 kΩ) compared to the others suggests a variation in manufacturing tolerances or simply a different batch, not necessarily a defect in your original units.

The critical flaw in relying solely on static multimeter readings is that these coils are designed to be driven dynamically. The PCM applies voltage to the primary side for a few milliseconds, then abruptly cuts power, causing the magnetic field to collapse and inducing thousands of volts in the secondary winding. A coil might measure perfectly within spec on a bench but fail under load due to internal shorts in the insulation or weak driver transistors inside the module that don't show up as resistance anomalies.

To truly rule out a bad coil, you must simulate the actual operating conditions rather than just checking continuity. The most reliable method is a live-fire diagnostic:
1.  Ensure the engine is at operating temperature.
2.  Clear any stored misfire codes to get a fresh baseline.
3.  Inspect the spark plug wires or boot integrity; poor connections can mimic coil failure.
4.  Swap coils between cylinders while monitoring the OBD-II data stream for real-time misfire counts (P030X codes).

If Cylinder 1 has a high misfire count and swapping in a known good coil moves that error code to Cylinder 2, you have isolated the faulty unit regardless of what your multimeter said. If the misfire persists on the same cylinder after multiple coil swaps, the fault likely lies with the spark plug, the wiring harness, or the PCM driver circuit itself.

Your data table actually shows excellent consistency across the original coils. The variation between 28 kΩ and 34 kΩ is well within normal manufacturing tolerances for aftermarket LS1 coils. The "outlier" in Coil #7 (61 kΩ on A-D) appears to be a measurement artifact or a specific terminal pair configuration rather than a total failure, especially since the other combinations remain consistent with the rest of the set.

In software development, we often debug by adding logs everywhere until we find the anomaly. In automotive diagnostics, adding more measurements isn't always better; sometimes you need to step back and understand the system architecture. The LS1 coil pack relies on precise timing and voltage spikes that a passive multimeter cannot replicate. Trusting the dynamic behavior of the engine under load provides a much higher confidence level than trusting static resistance values alone.

For those working on complex hardware diagnostics where component swapping isn't feasible, oscilloscopes become essential tools to visualize the dwell time and voltage spike shape. However, for most LS1 applications, a systematic swap test remains the gold standard because it directly correlates the electrical output to engine performance metrics.
